content: The assessment of rifapentine for pregnant women with latent tuberculosis infection, as well as its use for treatment shortening in patients with pulmonary tuberculosis, is under consideration. High-dose rifampicin and levofloxacin are being evaluated for pediatric tuberculosis meningitis, while high-dose isoniazid is being studied for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB). Delamanid is being investigated for its efficacy in treating MDR-TB in children, both with and without HIV. Mike Frick disclosed that his organization received non-commercial support for tracking investments in tuberculosis (TB) research and development, hosting a symposium at the UNION meeting, advocating for increased funding for TB research and access to evidence-based interventions, and managing a community research advisors group. Simon Schaaf reported receiving grants for pharmacokinetic drug studies in children involving second-line drugs and for studying preventive therapy in MDR-TB. Carrie Tudor stated that her organization receives funding from the Eli Lilly Foundation for activities related to TB and MDR-TB projects. Members of the External Review Group, including Riitta Dlodlo, Celine Garfin, Lee Reichman, Vaira Leimane, Rohit Sarin, Dalene von Delft, and Fraser Wares, declared no conflicts of interest related to the objectives of the meeting. WHO staff from regional offices, such as Masoud Dara (Europe), Mirtha del Granado (Americas), Daniel Kibuga (Africa), Hyder Khurshid (South-East Asia), Mohamed Aziz (Eastern Mediterranean), and Nobuyuki Nishikiori (Western Pacific), reviewed the final draft of the guideline document. Evidence reviewers, including Narges Alipanah, Cecily Miller, Payam Nahid (team leader for PICO 1, 2, and 7–10), and Lelia Chaisson from the University of California, San Francisco, and Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, respectively, contributed to systematic reviews. Richard Menzies (team leader for PICO 3, 4, and 6) from McGill University and James Johnston from the University of British Columbia also participated. Gregory Fox (team leader for PICO 11) and Jennifer Ho from the University of Sydney were involved as well. These reviewers did not participate in formulating policy recommendations. Some reviewers, such as Narges Alipanah, Jennifer Ho, and James Johnston, declared no conflicts of interest, while Payam Nahid disclosed that his research unit received support from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention for clinical trial units in San Francisco and Hanoi. The WHO guidelines on drug-resistant tuberculosis treatment were developed following the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development (2014) and the GRADE approach (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation). This methodology was used to assess the certainty of evidence and determine the strength of recommendations. The evidence was rated as high, moderate, low, or very low, and recommendations were classified as strong or conditional based on the balance of desirable and undesirable effects, values, preferences, resource use, equity considerations, acceptability, and feasibility. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) prepared for an in-person meeting on April 27, 2017, by drafting scoping and planning documents. A proposal was submitted to the WHO Guideline Review Committee (GRC) in February 2017 and approved in March 2017. Webinars were held to finalize scoping, establish PICO (Patients, Intervention, Comparator, and Outcomes) questions, and review evidence. The GDG reached decisions through unanimous agreement or consensus without voting. The quality of evidence was assessed based on factors such as risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and other considerations. Evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) was generally rated higher than observational studies. The GDG concluded that the certainty of evidence for isoniazid-resistant TB (Hr-TB) was low or very low due to residual confounding and data limitations, leading to conditional rather than strong recommendations. The guideline revision process included external review and incorporation of feedback. The GDG considered new data from observational studies, RCTs, and programmatic use of novel TB medicines like bedaquiline and delamanid. The 2018 update aimed to provide evidence-based guidance for MDR/RR-TB treatment, addressing patient and caregiver concerns about injectable agents, which often cause pain and serious adverse effects such as hearing loss and kidney dysfunction.
